en: When he sighed,
Blue flame burst above his head;
When wrath seized him,
His true strength split stone.
He halted in anger,
Appearing as a lion-prince,
And lamented his bloodthirsty father.
His gray-wolf ritual father,
Almambet, came to mind;
Your hero rolled over,
Coiling like a black snake.
Unable to endure his thoughts,
His old wound was stirred;
No mortal came within a handspan of him.
It was the time when he looked back
And counted his falcon uncle Syrgak.
It was the time when he counted him.
Straight ahead stood the house at Keng-Kol;
Do not ask the falcon's condition—
No wretched mortal came within a handspan.
At the treasury gate
He had the doolbas beaten;
When the doolbas was struck,
Its sound deafened the ears.
From the fortress with gates,
From Chachykei's palace,
From below Tört-Kül,
From the garden planted by his princely father Manas,
From opposite Bar-Köl,
From the garden planted by hero Manas,
Kanchoro and Külchoro—
For the two out among the horses,
The doolbas was beaten hard,
And the horses stampeded together.
Bounding and bunching like roe deer,
Külchoro and Kanchoro,
The two of them in great haste,
Readied and saddled their coursers,
Alarmed by Semetey:
"The doolbas has been beaten hard;
Its sound makes the ears ring.
Is there a trench already dug?!
Has an army engulfed us
From forty Kalmak tribes?!"
Unable to stand in their alarm,
The two companions raced,
Their stirrups striking together,
And rode into the palace.
There, wearing a blue lynx-fur cap
And wielding a blue-mottled shield,
Was old Bakai the gray wolf.
All their khans were there;
Gathered in the palace,
All the heroes were there,
And wise old Bakai.
His moonlike face gleaming,
Semetey spoke in a resounding voice.
He began his words to Khan Bakai,
Speaking softly but laying down firm resolve;
Your lion-prince began:
"We raided Andizhan,
Where blue caps perch high
And argamaks hold their heads proud;
We made horse-tails reach the knees,
And relentlessly sought the blood-price
Of my ritual father Chubak,
But nothing came of it.
We attacked Samarkand
And took much booty there.
We raided Tashkent and opened the road,
And brought humiliation upon many souls.
We followed the transmitted accounts
And asked those who knew;
Unable to learn Chubak's fate,
We withered long in humiliation.
The horses have grown fat and restless,
The heroes fat and pent-up;
For vigorous youths and swift horses,
The time has come to prove their worth.
They say there is no remedy against fate;
We stand seeking counsel
From you, uncle Bakai.
They say Kongurbai, who dwells
In Great Beijing,
Is a hero who broke the combined strength
Of a handful of Muslims;
A wise man among spearmen,
A lion born among the Chinese,
Who knows the enemy's stratagems.
A resourceful sage,
A hero guarding
Kakanchin's Beijing.
Those who fought him did not win.
No man has bent him down;
No mortal has dared face him.
None who confronted him remained alive.
His ox grew old and he himself died;
He divided evenly the property of the dead.
He raised his wether as a sacred offering,*
The horse he rode became holy,
And he remained apart from women.
He saddled his unbroken horse;
There was a great idol the size of a house,
And saying that this was God,
He bowed down precisely to it.
Kongurbai, khan of the monks—
Against that wrathful infidel,
Hero Khan Kongurbai,
Let us level our guns fiercely
And summon all our courage.
Let us gird our waists firmly
And pursue from the Kalcha in Beijing
The blood-price of my father!
Against the seething infidel,
Hero Khan Kongurbai,
That poor man in his full strength,
Let us enter directly and level our spears;
Let us finish and seize the infidel
And offer him as a sacrifice.
We have our forefather's vengeance;
Let us go straight in and take it!
Against the notorious infidel,
Hero Khan Kongurbai,
Let us make a mighty holy campaign.
If death reaches us, let us die;
Let us try to crush
The mighty and renowned infidel
Who slaughtered my father,
And see whether we can bear
The line God has drawn upon our necks.
If you lead the way, uncle,
To the hellish Black Chinese,
Let us try our strength against them.
Can there be a remedy against fate?
If death comes, let us die.
Breaking ranks in the spear-fight,
Falling to a bullet if fate arrives,
Bakburchun is where I shall enter;
Kakanchin is where I shall meet my end.
If I campaign against the infidel,
I stand ready to grapple
With hero Khan Kongurbai,
Who slaughtered my father!
I hear that even Chalyiar never touched
The city of Kakanchin.
I wish to thrust in my hand,
And clash in combat
With the formidable Kalcha!
If my strength suffices, I wish
To fight and avenge myself in Beijing!
My camel-like uncle, hear my words;
I entrust myself to Almighty Allah.
The Chinese slaughtered my father;
Uncle Bakai, hear my words—
How can I endure this grief!
Some people say
That no flood can pass
Through surging Beijing.
I wish to circle into the land
Of Beijing, which no flood can reach,
And unleash an upheaval;
I wish to avenge my father
Upon the surging Black infidel!
I hear that no prophet has gone
To imperial Great Beijing;
I wish to ride in and level my spear
In Beijing, where no prophet has trod!
I wish to pursue my father's blood-price
From the vile Black Chinese.
They call it Chin-Machin, they call it Kakan—
How many names does Beijing have?
Those sovereign Chinese
Have slaughtered valiant heroes.
Lion uncle, hear my words:
What great worth lies in battle!
Against Beijing of Chin-Machin,
I long to wage a true holy war,
Strike their horses in a swift raid,
And drive them back this way!
Upon that people, numerous as ants,
I long to descend upon their heads.
Kongurbai is their prince;
I long to drink his blood!
Against the teeming Chinese khagan,
I long to unleash utter turmoil.
Against the black-hearted infidel,
I long to exchange blows once.
The enemy I shall grapple is Kakan-Chyn;
I long to return having taken revenge.
If my death comes from God,
I long to die while fighting!
Some people tell tales;
Who knows whether they are false or true?
That Beijing, whence those who go do not return,
They call a place of calamity and hardship.
With my uncle as commander,
I long to enter that Beijing.
The countless dark livestock gathered as tribute—
I long to pour down upon them headlong.
If the one God grants good fortune,
I long to ride forth and enter against the foe!
Dearer than a child was
This Külchoro standing here;
Against the teeming Black Chinese,
I long to unleash him!
Sated with flowing blood,
Standing and fighting without fleeing,
Of the swaggering Black Chinese,
I long to break apart many cities.
If I do not take revenge, this wretched soul
Would rather die than go on living!
They have Kalmaks and Shivei,
And peoples of many kinds;
Among those peoples
Are giants of many kinds.
Fighting them satisfies one's longing;
Clashing with them sets the soul aflame.
They themselves follow the Chinese faith;
Kongurbai is khan of the Kechil.
However mighty that infidel may be,
He is our enemy to the core.
From the blustering infidel,
Let us shake the bullets from his quiver,
And test ourselves in combat.
Let us shout and thrust our spears,
And satisfy every battle hunger.
Do not mortals destined to die, die?
The decree God has written—
Will this entrusted, barren soul not see it?
When the Almighty gives the command,
Saying, ‘Your entrusted life is required,’
When the angel Azrael
Truly extends his five fingers,
The speaking tongue will be bound;
From this seven-day world,
What soul can flee and escape?
Will the dug grave not receive us?
Will the black earth not cover us?
The foe we shall grapple is Kakan-Chyn;
We shall somehow find his weakness,
Our lion father who passed into Judgment Day—
We shall avenge him by destroying them.
Even if almighty God has decreed
Our fate in Beijing,
We shall bring fierce turmoil there.
The road to Beijing divides five ways;
The Kalcha who has cut down every hero
Is himself a peerless warrior.
If I do not ceaselessly scout the road,
If I do not go to demand the blood-price
Of my mountain-like godfather,
May I sink away as though never born;
Rather than go on living feebly,
Let me die instead.
The infidel son of Kaldai,
Hero Khan Kongurbai—
